items.title: Mauvaise Foi
items.question: In Sartre's philosophy, what does the French term for self-deception about one's own freedom describe?
items.correctAnswer: Bad faith
items.correctExplanation: Right. It names the flight from freedom by pretending our choices are not ours.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is bad faith. The self-deception hides from the very freedom that defines us.
items.lessonContent:
Self-deception can be a philosophical stance.
We may deny our own freedom to escape responsibility.
Naming the evasion is the first step past it.
Notice where you claim you had no choice.
Share this: catch one moment today when you said you had no choice.

items.title: Forced Freedom
items.question: What does Sartre mean by saying humans are condemned to be free?
choices: Freedom is a punishment from others
People are never free in practice
items.correctAnswer: Freedom cannot be escaped
items.correctExplanation: Right. We did not choose to be free, yet we cannot stop choosing, even by refusing.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is freedom cannot be escaped. Even refusing to choose is itself a choice, which is the weight he describes.
items.lessonContent:
Some conditions arrive without consent.
Even refusal is a decision.
Responsibility follows from unavoidable choice.
Own the choices you would rather deny.
Share this: note one refusal that was itself a decision.

items.title: Existence First
items.question: What does the slogan that existence precedes essence mean for humans?
choices: We are born with a fixed nature
items.correctAnswer: We create ourselves through choices
items.correctExplanation: Right. Unlike a manufactured object, a person first exists and then defines what they are through action.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is we create ourselves through choices. There is no blueprint to fall back on, which is both the freedom and the burden.
items.lessonContent:
Some things are made to a plan.
People are not; they become through action.
No fixed nature excuses a choice.
Self-definition is ongoing work.
Share this: name one trait you are actively choosing rather than inheriting.

items.title: The Waiter
items.question: Why does Sartre use a café waiter to illustrate bad faith?
choices: He performs his role as if it fixed him
He refuses to work at all
He has no freedom to choose
items.correctAnswer: He performs his role as if it fixed him
items.correctExplanation: Right. The waiter plays at being a waiter, treating a role as an inescapable essence rather than a chosen activity.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is he performs his role as if it fixed him. The exaggerated performance reveals the flight from freedom into a persona.
items.lessonContent:
Roles can become hiding places.
Playing a part rigidly may mask a choice.
Distinguish what you do from what you are.
Notice when a role does your deciding.
Share this: observe one role you slip into as an escape.

items.title: Anguish of Choice
items.question: What kind of distress does Sartre associate with recognising our freedom?
items.correctAnswer: Anxiety about responsibility
items.correctExplanation: Right. Facing that we alone author our choices produces a vertigo of responsibility.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is anxiety about responsibility. It is not fear of harm but the weight of being the source of one's own values.
items.lessonContent:
Freedom carries weight.
Responsibility can feel like vertigo.
Anxiety is a signal of authorship.
Do not let it push you into denial.
Share this: sit with one decision you are avoiding out of its weight.

items.title: No Excuses
items.question: What does Sartre say about blaming one's nature or upbringing for one's actions?
choices: It is a form of bad faith
items.correctAnswer: It is a form of bad faith
items.correctExplanation: Right. Explaining ourselves away through causes denies the freedom that remains regardless of background.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is it is a form of bad faith. Background shapes the situation, yet the response to it is still chosen.
items.lessonContent:
Causes can explain without excusing.
Circumstances set the scene, not the answer.
Watch for explanations that erase agency.
Acknowledge influence without surrendering choice.
Share this: separate one influence on you from the choice you still make.

items.title: Being for Itself
items.question: What does Sartre mean by consciousness being for-itself rather than in-itself?
choices: It is a fixed physical object
It has no existence at all
items.correctAnswer: It is aware and self-transcending
items.correctExplanation: Right. Consciousness is not a thing that simply is; it is directed beyond itself and aware of its own awareness.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is it is aware and self-transcending. Objects are in themselves, while consciousness always relates to something beyond it.
items.lessonContent:
Two modes of being can be distinguished.
Things simply are; awareness relates.
Consciousness is always about something.
Distinguish substance from activity.
Share this: notice how your attention is always directed at something.

items.title: Fixed Facts
items.question: What does Sartre call the facts about our situation that we did not choose?
items.correctAnswer: Facticity
items.correctExplanation: Right. Birth, body, and past are given facts that limit without determining us.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is facticity. It names what is simply given, as opposed to what we do with it.
items.lessonContent:
Some givens cannot be chosen.
Limits are real but not total.
Distinguish the given from the response.
Work within facts without surrendering to them.
Share this: list one unchangeable fact and one choice it still leaves open.

items.title: Going Beyond
items.question: What does Sartre call our capacity to surpass the given facts of our situation?
items.correctAnswer: Transcendence
items.correctExplanation: Right. We can project beyond what is given, which is the active side of freedom.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is transcendence. It is the movement past the fixed toward what we make of it.
items.lessonContent:
Facts are not the whole story.
We project beyond the given.
Freedom lies in the surpassing.
Balance limits with possibility.
Share this: name one way you could surpass a limit you currently accept.

items.title: Living Truthfully
items.question: What does Sartre call the attitude that owns one's freedom and responsibility?
items.correctAnswer: Authenticity
items.correctExplanation: Right. Authentic existence acknowledges that one is the author of one's choices.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is authenticity. It is not a permanent state but an ongoing honesty about one's freedom.
items.lessonContent:
Honesty with oneself is a practice.
Own your authorship.
It is a direction, not a finished badge.
Return to it after lapses.
Share this: name one area where you will own your choices this week.

items.title: Life Project
items.question: What does Sartre mean by a fundamental project?
items.correctAnswer: An overarching choice of self
items.correctExplanation: Right. Beneath particular choices lies a basic orientation that gives them shape.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is an overarching choice of self. The project unifies many decisions into a coherent direction.
items.lessonContent:
Many choices can share a theme.
A unifying direction shapes particular acts.
Review the pattern behind your decisions.
Adjust the project, not just the steps.
Share this: name the direction most of your recent choices point toward.

items.title: Serious World
items.question: What does Sartre criticise in the attitude that treats values as fixed objects in the world?
choices: It hides human authorship of values
It respects other people too much
items.correctAnswer: It hides human authorship of values
items.correctExplanation: Right. Treating values as given things avoids the burden of having chosen them.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is it hides human authorship of values. Projecting our values outward lets us claim they were imposed rather than chosen.
items.lessonContent:
Values can be treated as discovered facts.
That framing hides the choices behind them.
Owning authorship is uncomfortable.
See values as commitments, not objects.
Share this: name one value you hold and the choice that sustains it.

items.title: Determinism Excuse
items.question: Why does Sartre consider a rigid belief in determinism a form of bad faith?
choices: It denies the freedom we experience
items.correctAnswer: It denies the freedom we experience
items.correctExplanation: Right. Using causality as an excuse pretends that our deliberation makes no difference.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is it denies the freedom we experience. The belief conveniently removes responsibility for what we do.
items.lessonContent:
An excuse can take a philosophical form.
Denying choice removes accountability.
Notice when theory serves avoidance.
Hold explanations and agency together.
Share this: find one belief that conveniently excuses a habit.

items.title: The Look
items.question: What happens to a person when they become aware of being looked at by another, in Sartre's account?
choices: They become an object for the other
items.correctAnswer: They become an object for the other
items.correctExplanation: Right. Being seen turns us into something judged, introducing a tension between subject and object.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is they become an object for the other. The gaze reveals that others define us in ways we cannot control.
items.lessonContent:
Others see us in ways we cannot fully govern.
Being looked at changes self-awareness.
Identity is partly shaped from outside.
Balance inner authorship with outer perception.
Share this: notice how you change when someone is watching.

items.title: Shared Responsibility
items.question: Why does Sartre say that choosing for oneself is also choosing for humanity?
choices: A choice models a universal norm
No one is ever truly free
items.correctAnswer: A choice models a universal norm
items.correctExplanation: Right. In choosing, we affirm that this is how one ought to act, which carries weight beyond ourselves.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a choice models a universal norm. Every act tacitly proposes an example, which is why responsibility is so heavy.
items.lessonContent:
Personal choices imply general claims.
Acting suggests what others should do too.
Responsibility extends beyond yourself.
Weigh the example your action sets.
Share this: consider what example one of your habits sets for others.

items.title: The Coward
items.question: How does Sartre treat the person who claims to have been born a coward?
choices: They are not cowardly by nature
items.correctAnswer: They are not cowardly by nature
items.correctExplanation: Right. He says people make themselves cowardly through their acts, not by an inborn essence.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is they are not cowardly by nature. The claim of a fixed disposition is exactly the bad faith he criticises.
items.lessonContent:
Character is made through action.
Labels of fixed nature excuse inaction.
People can remake what they have become.
See traits as patterns, not essences.
Share this: name one trait you think you cannot change, and test it.

items.title: Paradox of Sincerity
items.question: Why is sincerity alone not sufficient to escape bad faith for Sartre?
choices: It can become a new fixed role
items.correctAnswer: It can become a new fixed role
items.correctExplanation: Right. Being true to a supposed fixed self can itself be a way of dodging change and responsibility.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is it can become a new fixed role. Clinging to a permanent identity can be as evasive as any other form of self-deception.
items.lessonContent:
Even virtues can become escapes.
A fixed self-image can prevent growth.
Watch for identities that block change.
Stay open to revising who you are.
Share this: question one label you use to explain yourself.

items.title: Committed Freedom
items.question: How does Sartre connect freedom with commitment?
choices: Freedom is realised through engaged choice
items.correctAnswer: Freedom is realised through engaged choice
items.correctExplanation: Right. Freedom is not idle detachment but the act of committing to something in the world.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is freedom is realised through engaged choice. Withdrawing from all commitment would be another evasion of responsibility.
items.lessonContent:
Freedom needs engagement to be real.
Choosing to do nothing is still a choice.
Commitment gives freedom direction.
Avoid the flight into detachment.
Share this: commit to one small thing you have been holding back from.

items.title: Situated Choice
items.question: What does Sartre mean by saying freedom is situated?
items.correctAnswer: Choice always occurs within limits
items.correctExplanation: Right. We choose within circumstances we did not pick, so freedom is always concrete rather than abstract.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is choice always occurs within limits. The situation shapes the options without eliminating the act of choosing.
items.lessonContent:
Freedom works through particular conditions.
Constraints shape the options available.
A limited field still requires choosing.
Do not confuse limits with absence of choice.
Share this: name one constraint and the choice it still allows.

items.title: Hell Is Others
items.question: What did Sartre mean by the famous line that hell is other people?
choices: Others fix us in their judgments
items.correctAnswer: Others fix us in their judgments
items.correctExplanation: Right. The line concerns how the gaze of others can freeze us into identities we did not choose.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is others fix us in their judgments. It is a claim about the power of being seen, not a condemnation of company.
items.lessonContent:
Others can define us against our will.
Judgment fixes what we feel is fluid.
The line is about the gaze, not hatred.
Notice when others' views trap you.
Share this: reflect on one label others place on you.

items.title: Free Refusal
items.question: Could someone escape freedom by refusing to choose at all, according to Sartre?
choices: No, refusing is itself a choice
Yes, if they try hard enough
items.correctAnswer: No, refusing is itself a choice
items.correctExplanation: Right. Declining to decide is a way of deciding, so freedom cannot be dodged.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is no, refusing is itself a choice. Even passivity expresses a stance, which is why responsibility cannot be evaded.
items.lessonContent:
Inaction expresses a stance.
Avoidance is a form of action.
You cannot step outside choosing.
Accept that passivity has consequences.
Share this: notice one non-decision that has already made a choice for you.

items.title: Without a Script
items.question: What does Sartre call the condition of being responsible for everything without having chosen one's existence?
items.correctAnswer: Abandonment
items.correctExplanation: Right. Without pre-given guidance, we are left to create values ourselves, which brings both freedom and forlornness.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is abandonment. It names the vertigo of having no fixed rulebook to lean on.
items.lessonContent:
Absence of guidance is a condition.
Freedom can feel like forlornness.
We must generate values without a script.
Accept the discomfort rather than flee it.
Share this: name one area where you must supply the rule yourself.

items.title: Choosing Self
items.question: What does Sartre say we are continually doing through our choices?
items.correctAnswer: Making ourselves
items.correctExplanation: Right. Each decision contributes to the person we are becoming, with no blueprint to follow.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is making ourselves. The self is the sum of choices rather than a pre-existing given.
items.lessonContent:
The self is built through action.
Choices accumulate into character.
No blueprint relieves us of authorship.
Attend to the pattern of your decisions.
Share this: name one small choice that is shaping who you are.

items.title: Roles and Freedom
items.question: How should one hold a social role, on Sartre's view?
choices: As a chosen performance to own
As the whole of one's identity
items.correctAnswer: As a chosen performance to own
items.correctExplanation: Right. Roles can be played consciously without being mistaken for one's entire essence.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is as a chosen performance to own. Treating the role as an unchangeable fate is precisely the bad faith he warns against.
items.lessonContent:
Roles are performances, not essences.
Play them without being swallowed.
Awareness keeps freedom intact.
Separate the part from the person.
Share this: name one role you play and how you might hold it more consciously.

items.title: Responsibility Weight
items.question: Why is authenticity difficult to sustain, according to Sartre?
choices: It means constant awareness of freedom
items.correctAnswer: It means constant awareness of freedom
items.correctExplanation: Right. Living without the comfort of excuses is demanding, so bad faith is a constant temptation.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is it means constant awareness of freedom. The difficulty is the ongoing responsibility, not any material condition.
items.lessonContent:
Honesty with oneself takes effort.
Comfortable excuses are tempting.
Authenticity is a continual return.
Expect lapses without abandoning the effort.
Share this: recommit to one honest choice you have been avoiding.
